papers.title: Incorporating the Knowledge Distillation to Improve the EfficientNet Transfer Learning Capability
papers.label: arXiv:2611.34025v1

summary.one_liner: The paper proposes using knowledge distillation to pass knowledge from larger EfficientNet models into smaller EfficientNet models as a transfer learning method for computer vision.
summary.plain: Image-recognition AI models are often pretrained on a large image collection and then reused for new tasks, a practice called transfer learning. This paper asks whether the smaller models in the EfficientNet family can be improved by learning from the larger models, which they were originally grown from. The authors report that this approach improved each EfficientNet size they tested, and that several smaller models beat a larger model trained the standard way.
summary.why: It offers a practical way to get better results from smaller, cheaper vision models without changing their size, which may matter for devices with limited computing power. The text is a short abstract, so it does not show how large or consistent the gains were, or how the method compares with other transfer approaches.
summary.background:
- Transfer learning: reusing a model trained on a large dataset (such as ImageNet) as the starting point for a new task.
- EfficientNet: a family of image-recognition networks of increasing size, where larger members were built by scaling up a smaller baseline.
- Knowledge distillation: training a smaller "student" model to imitate the outputs of a larger "teacher" model.
- ImageNet: a large benchmark dataset of labeled photographs used to compare vision models.

papers.abstract: Due to the Deep Learning requirement for a large training dataset, Transfer Learning has become a central method in the field of Computer Vision, which heavily used Deep Learning. Since the adoption of transfer learning in the field, the performance of the models in computer vision is significantly upgraded. The common transfer learning practice in computer vision research is to use state-of-the-art architectures in the ImageNet dataset as the backbone network. The best performing architecture in ImageNet is currently held by EfficientNet, which is a set of architectures that were progressively grown from a baseline architecture. By observing the EfficientNet development approach, it is natural to hypothesize that the smaller EfficientNet architecture is capable to contain the knowledge of the larger architecture. This hypothesis comes from the fact that the larger EfficientNet architecture was grown from the smaller architecture. Therefore, in this study, we experimented if it is beneficial to transfer the knowledge from the larger architecture to the smaller architecture of the EfficientNet. To achieve this goal, we proposed a transfer learning method that uses Knowledge Distillation as the knowledge transfer mechanism from the larger to smaller architecture. We found that the proposed method is able to upgrade the performance of each of the EfficientNet architecture. Several smaller architectures are even able to outperform the larger architecture that was trained using the standard transfer learning method.

papers.title: TAT-Det: A Dataset for Testicular Appendage Torsion Detection and Segmentation in Ultrasound Images
papers.label: arXiv:2611.33940v1

summary.one_liner: TAT-Det is a publicly described ultrasound dataset of 2,600 expert-annotated images from 1,203 children, with bounding boxes and pixel masks for testicular appendage torsion, plus baseline detection and segmentation benchmarks.
summary.plain: This paper is about a painful condition in young boys called testicular appendage torsion, a small twisted tissue structure in the scrotum that is a common cause of sudden scrotal pain before puberty. The authors built a labeled set of 2,600 ultrasound images from 1,203 patients at a children's hospital in China, with outlines drawn by trained specialists. They then tested several existing AI models on the images, reporting that YOLO11m performed best at finding the lesion and RWKV-UNet performed best at outlining it.
summary.why: Pediatric scrotal emergencies are hard to diagnose from symptoms alone, and there were few public datasets for this problem, so a shared labeled resource could let other groups build and compare automated tools. The text does not report how these models would perform in clinical use, so its practical value remains to be tested.
summary.background:
- Testicular appendage torsion (TAT): twisting of a tiny appendage attached to the testicle; the leading cause of sudden scrotal pain in prepubertal boys.
- Ultrasound: sound-wave imaging used to look inside the body without radiation.
- Dataset annotation: human experts marking the region of interest in each image so software can learn from it.
- Bounding box vs. segmentation mask: a rectangle around a lesion (detection) versus a pixel-by-pixel outline of it (segmentation).
- Baseline benchmark: a first set of reference scores that later methods can be compared against.
- YOLO11m and RWKV-UNet: names of existing deep learning model architectures used for detection and segmentation respectively.

papers.abstract: Background: Testicular appendage torsion (TAT) is the leading cause of acute scrotal pain in prepubertal children. Yet, its diagnosis remains challenging due to nonspecific clinical manifestations and the absence of standardized datasets for pediatric acute scrotal emergencies. Results: We present TAT-Det, an expert-annotated ultrasound dataset specifically designed for TAT. TAT-Det comprises 2,600 ultrasound images from 1,203 patients collected at the Children's Hospital, Zhejiang University School of Medicine. Each TAT-positive image is accompanied by lesion-level bounding boxes for detection and pixel-level segmentation masks for fine-grained delineation. Annotations were produced through a multi-stage workflow involving independent annotation by board-certified pediatric sonographers, consensus review, and refinement. Baseline benchmarks for object detection and semantic segmentation using representative deep learning models are further provided, with YOLO11m achieving the best detection performance and RWKV-UNet the best segmentation performance. Conclusions: TAT-Det addresses the lack of publicly available resources for pediatric emergency ultrasound and establishes a foundation for developing and evaluating artificial intelligence methods for automated TAT analysis.

papers.title: Visual-State Graph Memory for Streaming Video Understanding
papers.label: arXiv:2611.32369v1

summary.background:
- Vision-language model (VLM): an AI system that answers questions about images or video given as input.
- Streaming video: video that arrives continuously, so the model sees it frame by frame and cannot look ahead.
- Scene graph: a structured description of a scene as nodes (objects) connected by edges (relations such as "holding" or "next to").
- Training-free: the method is added on top of existing models without retraining them.
- Input budget: a fixed limit on how much information (e.g., number of frames or tokens) the model can take in at once.
- Retrieval: selecting only the stored items relevant to the current question.
summary.one_liner: Proposes Visual-State Graph (VSG), a training-free memory for streaming video that stores objects, their relations, and an event log as a persistent, dynamically updated scene graph, and retrieves from it alongside recent frames under a fixed input budget.
summary.plain: Video models often need to answer questions about something that happened earlier in a long live video, but the important moment may have scrolled out of their short window of recent frames. This paper proposes a memory that keeps a running summary of the scene instead of every frame: each object gets one lasting entry with a dated history of how it changed, plus a log of events. When a question arrives, the system pulls out the relevant objects and events together with the latest frames.
summary.why: Streaming video applications such as monitoring or assistive devices need to recall the past without storing unlimited footage, so a compact memory of scene state is a practical design question. The text reports that, across four benchmarks and seven open-source vision-language models (7B to 32B parameters), VSG improved reasoning about the past under matched input budgets while keeping real-time operation; the size and consistency of these gains beyond the abstract are not described here.

papers.abstract: In streaming video understanding, the evidence needed to answer a question may have already left the recent-frame window. Keeping all frames does not scale with video length, while dropping older frames limits the model's ability to reason about the past. We propose Visual-State Graph (VSG), a training-free memory that stores the state of a stream rather than the raw sequence of frames. VSG represents the stream as a graph of objects and their relations, together with a log of events; similar to a dynamically evolving scene graph. An object observed repeatedly is represented by one persistent node, with a timestamped history of how its state changes. To determine whether a newly mentioned object already exists in the graph, we compare the relations it takes part in with those of stored objects. We build this memory as the video arrives, before the questions are known. When a question arrives, we retrieve relevant objects and events alongside recent frames under a fixed input budget. Our evaluation spans four streaming-video benchmarks and seven open-source vision-language models ranging from 7B to 32B parameters. Under matched input budgets, VSG improves reasoning about the past while preserving real-time understanding.

papers.title: DOPER: Deep Object Pose Estimation Revisited
papers.label: arXiv:2611.32846v1

summary.background:
- Pose estimation: finding an object's 3D position and rotation (6D pose) relative to the camera.
- Keypoints and heatmaps: a few marked points on the object, and a map of how likely each point is to be at each pixel.
- Perspective-n-Point (PnP): a standard calculation that turns matched 2D image points and known 3D model points into a pose.
- Synthetic training: learning from computer-rendered images rather than real photos, then adapting to real ones.
- CAD model: a digital 3D design of the object.
- Multi-view and calibration: using several cameras whose positions are precisely known.
- Average precision (AP): a standard score for how well detections match the true objects.
summary.one_liner: DOPER is an RGB-only framework that shares one visual backbone across detection, segmentation, and keypoint prediction to estimate 6D object poses via Perspective-n-Point, trained from synthetic data and adapted to real images with partial supervision and multi-view geometric constraints.
summary.plain: This paper is about working out where a known object is and how it is turned in 3D, using only ordinary color camera images. The method first learns from computer-generated images, then adapts to real photos, and it locates points on the object to compute its position and orientation. The authors report state-of-the-art detection scores on four benchmark datasets and real-time speed (about 35 times per second per object).
summary.why: Estimating object pose from a plain camera matters for robotics and spacecraft or warehouse tasks where depth sensors are not available. The text claims state-of-the-art detection accuracy and real-time speed, but the summary alone does not show how these compare to other methods in detail.

papers.abstract: We present DOPER, an RGB pose estimation framework that shares a visual backbone across object detection, segmentation, and keypoint prediction to recover the 6D pose of known objects through Perspective-n-Point. Starting from synthetic training, DOPER adapts to real observations using partial supervision while retaining synthetic keypoint labels. Calibrated multi-view observations provide geometric constraints for keypoint supervision. During inference, optional heatmap refinement fits a rigid pose directly to the predicted keypoint distributions, resolving ambiguous correspondences without depth input or a learned pose refiner. Starting from underspecified CAD models, DOPER progressively refines the object representation and pose estimator. Results on SPEED+ and SHIRT further demonstrate effective adaptation to illumination changes and accurate temporal pose estimation. Across the evaluated single-view and multi-view configurations, DOPER achieves state-of-the-art detection AP results on HANDAL, HOPEv2, HOT3D, and T-LESS while using only RGB and running in real time (35 Hz per object model on one GB300). These results demonstrate the effectiveness of jointly learning detection and pose keypoints, with real observations and geometric constraints.

papers.title: Benchmarking VLM Medical Hallucination across 5 Modalities
papers.label: arXiv:2611.29934v1

summary.background:
- Vision-language model (VLM): an AI system that takes both an image and a text question and produces a text answer.
- Hallucination: when an AI states something confidently that is not supported by its input, such as describing a finding that is absent from a scan.
- Benchmark: a standard set of test questions used to compare systems fairly.
- Imaging modality: the type of medical image, such as X-ray, MRI, CT, or ultrasound.
- Statistical significance: whether a difference in scores is likely real rather than due to chance in a limited test.
- The abstract does not name the five modalities or the four question categories, so those details are not covered here.
summary.one_liner: Introduces Multi-Med, a 1,000-item medical hallucination benchmark spanning five imaging modalities, and uses it to evaluate 10 vision-language models across four question categories.
summary.plain: Vision-language models are AI systems that answer questions about images, and they sometimes make up details that the picture does not show. This paper builds a test set of 1,000 medical image and question pairs covering five kinds of medical imaging, then checks how 10 popular models perform. The authors report that accuracy varies a lot by imaging type and question type, while the top models are not clearly different from one another statistically.
summary.why: Medical AI tools that describe scans can be wrong in ways that matter, so knowing where they fail is useful for deciding where they can be trusted. The text does not say how the benchmark will be used beyond this study, so its wider impact is unclear.

papers.abstract: Hallucinations in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) within the medical domain remain a difficult and not well-understood problem, and it is still unclear where these models break down. Although several benchmarks targeting medical hallucination have been introduced, they often lack broad coverage across different medical imaging modalities. We introduce Multi-Med, a medical hallucination benchmark containing 1,000 image-question pairs spanning five distinct modalities. Using this benchmark, we perform an in-depth experimental study of 10 widely used VLMs across five modalities and four question categories. Our findings indicate that model performance differs substantially depending on the imaging modality and question type, and that the differences among the best-performing models are not statistically significant.

papers.title: SVUBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Proactive Streaming Video Understanding
papers.label: arXiv:2611.30541v1

summary.background:
- Streaming video: video that arrives continuously, so the model sees only the past and present, not the full clip.
- Proactive response: the model decides on its own when to answer, rather than waiting for a question.
- Benchmark: a standardized test set used to compare models fairly.
- Answer window: the time span during which an answer counts as on time.
- Historical recovery: recalling relevant earlier moments in the video to answer correctly.
- Duration tiers: the test groups videos by length to see how performance changes as videos get longer.
summary.one_liner: SVUBench is a benchmark of about 12,000 questions across ten tasks for testing whether video models can proactively respond to unfolding streaming video, using a new Proactive Response Score that accounts for correctness, timeliness, historical consistency, and content quality.
summary.plain: This paper introduces a test set for AI systems that watch live or streaming video and must speak up at the right moment, rather than only answering questions after a clip has finished. The benchmark has over 12,000 questions and about 63,000 answer points, built with help from AI models and checked by humans. The authors also propose a scoring method that judges not just whether answers are right, but whether they arrive on time and stay consistent with earlier events.
summary.why: Streaming video assistants, such as those that monitor a camera feed and alert a user, need to act in real time, and standard benchmarks do not measure that well. The paper reports that extensive experiments reveal strengths and limitations of existing models, but the text does not give specific results, so its practical impact is not yet clear from this summary alone.

papers.abstract: Proactive streaming video understanding requires models to interpret unfolding events, respond timely, and retrieve relevant historical evidence. To systematically evaluate these capabilities, we introduce SVUBench, a comprehensive proactive streaming video benchmark comprising 12,131 questions and 62,881 answer points across ten proactive tasks spanning Perception, Understanding, and Reasoning. Constructed through model-assisted annotation and human verification, SVUBench introduces two complementary interaction modes. Basic evaluates sustained proactive responses from video onset, while Trajectory requires historical recovery and continuous response updates following task activation during streaming. A Duration-Scaled Challenge further evaluates these capabilities across four video duration tiers. We develop the Proactive Response Score (PRS) with task-adaptive answer windows to jointly assess answer correctness, response timeliness, historical consistency, and content quality. Extensive experiments and analysis reveal the strengths and limitations of existing models, highlighting directions for advancing proactive streaming video understanding.

papers.title: PP-CFG: Polarity-Preserving Guidance for Controllable Few-Step Image and Video Generation
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27266v1

summary.background:
- Diffusion models generate images or videos by starting from noise and removing it over many denoising steps.
- Distillation trains a faster "student" model with few steps to imitate a slower "teacher" model.
- Classifier-free guidance (CFG) is a dial that controls how strongly the output follows a text prompt.
- Negative prompts tell the model what to leave out of the output.
- Attention is the mechanism through which parts of the model weigh and combine information from the text and image.
- VBench is a standard benchmark suite for scoring video generation quality.
- Distribution matching distillation (DMD) and latent consistency models (LCM) are two specific distillation techniques named in the paper.
summary.one_liner: PP-CFG is a few-step diffusion distillation method that keeps positive and negative text conditions separate, combines their attention responses with opposite signs, and uses a scale-and-timestep mixer to keep adjustable classifier-free guidance and negative prompting for image and video generation.
summary.plain: Modern AI image and video generators often need many small refinement steps to produce output, and speeding them up by distilling them into fewer steps tends to remove the ability to fine-tune how strongly a prompt is followed or to tell the model what to avoid. This paper proposes a way to keep those controls in a four-step student model. The authors report results on video (Wan2.1) and image (Qwen-Image) generators, including a VBench score of 81.46 in four steps and higher target-removal rates on their own 1,000-case negative-prompt benchmark than the teacher models.
summary.why: Making generation both fast and controllable is a practical bottleneck for image and video tools, so a method that preserves guidance and negative prompts in few-step models is worth watching. The text supports claims across two backbones and two distillation methods, but the evaluation is described only at a high level and the benchmark is the authors' own, so the strength of the generality claim is not yet established.

papers.abstract: Few-step diffusion distillation reduces sampling cost but often weakens adjustable classifier-free guidance (CFG) and runtime negative prompting. We introduce PP-CFG, an architecture that keeps positive and negative text conditions separate and combines their attention responses with opposite signs within a shared visual backbone. Its Scale-Time Polarity Mixer refines each condition using the guidance scale and denoising timestep, allowing prompt influence to vary throughout generation. The student retains a continuous scale input and selectable negative prompts with one visual backbone pass per step. We evaluate PP-CFG on Wan2.1 for video generation with distribution matching distillation (DMD), and on Qwen-Image with both latent consistency model (LCM) distillation and DMD. PP-CFG achieves 81.46 VBench in four steps and lower video teacher-student distances across guidance scales than step-distilled DMD. On NegElement-1K, our benchmark of 1,000 matched image and video prompt cases, it achieves higher target-removal rates than the corresponding teachers. These experiments support the method's generality across attention architectures, generation modalities, and distillation objectives while retaining competitive generation quality.

papers.title: Learning 3D MRI Representations with Generative Adversarial Networks
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27057v1

summary.background:
- Representation learning: training a model to turn raw data into compact numerical features that other tasks can use.
- Reconstruction-based learning: learning by trying to rebuild the original input from its compressed form, with no human labels needed.
- Contrastive learning: learning by pulling similar examples together and pushing different ones apart in feature space; a common alternative.
- CNN (convolutional neural network): a common type of image model that detects local patterns; a 3D version works on volumes rather than flat images.
- GAN (generative adversarial network): two networks trained against each other, one generating images and one judging them, often used to make outputs look realistic.
- MRI: magnetic resonance imaging, which produces 3D scans of soft tissue such as the brain.
- Parkinson's and Alzheimer's classification: deciding from scans whether a patient has these diseases, used here as a test of the learned features.
summary.one_liner: The paper proposes R2RG, a 3D CNN-based representation learning method that uses an auto-encoding GAN and a composite loss to learn reconstruction-based features from 3D MRI scans with limited data, reporting gains over contrastive methods on Parkinson's and Alzheimer's classification.
summary.plain: Medical scans like MRI are 3D, but many AI methods handle only flat 2D slices, which throws away depth information, and they often need more data than medical datasets provide. This paper presents a method that learns compact summaries of whole 3D brain MRI volumes by training a network to rebuild the scans, with a generative adversarial network (a pair of AI models that compete to make realistic images) helping sharpen the rebuilt results. The authors report that these learned summaries work across several datasets, including small ones, and perform better than certain competing approaches on Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease classification.
summary.why: Many medical AI tasks have little labelled data, so methods that learn useful features without labels could matter in clinical research. The text reports results on a few datasets, but it does not show how well the approach would hold up in routine clinical use, so its wider significance is still to be tested.

papers.abstract: Learning representations of visual images is a challenging task. It requires extracting abstract patterns from high-dimensional data without explicit supervision. This becomes pronounced with 3D MR imaging due to sparse features, higher dimensional inputs, and smaller datasets. Many state-of-the-art representation learning algorithms successfully rely on transformers and diffusion-based architectures. However, these methods struggle with smaller datasets. In effect, solution methods relax the problem by slicing 3D volumes and solving the problem for 2D medical imaging, resulting in a loss of spatial 3D information. We present R2RG, a representation learning method based on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), with Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) honing the reconstruction task. Our key insights lie in exploiting architectural biases in 3D CNNs, combined with data-efficient auto-encoding GANs and a composite loss function to enhance reconstruction fidelity and stabilize training. Our experiments on three standard datasets and a locally collected dataset show that R2RG not only achieves superior performance but also generalizes to heterogeneous and smaller datasets. Furthermore, representations learned with R2RG outperform those learned with contrastive-based representation learning methods on Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease classification. Our work demonstrates that reconstruction-based representation learning is a promising direction for 3D medical imaging under limited data availability.

papers.title: Digitization of Analogue Gauges using Computer Vision
papers.label: arXiv:2611.26262v1

summary.background:
- Analogue gauge: a dial with a needle that shows a measured value, such as pressure in BAR (a unit of pressure).
- Computer vision: methods that let computers extract information from images.
- OpenCV and Scikit-Image: standard software libraries for image processing; here they are used for traditional, hand-designed steps.
- Deep learning: training a neural network on many examples instead of writing rules by hand.
- ResNet18 and VGG19: two named neural network designs; ResNet uses "residual" shortcut connections, which the authors credit for their result.
- Data augmentation: creating extra training images by altering existing ones (rotating, adjusting brightness, etc.).
- Industry 5.0: a term for factory strategies that combine automation with human-centred goals.
summary.one_liner: The paper compares three hybrid pipelines (OpenCV with Scikit-Image, OpenCV with ResNet18, OpenCV with VGG19) for automatically reading 0-10 BAR pressure gauges from images, using a 1,848-image dataset built from web scraping, synthetic generation, and augmentation.
summary.plain: Many factories still use dial-style pressure gauges that people read by eye, which is slow and prone to mistakes. This paper tests whether a computer can read these dials from photos, comparing three methods on a set of pressure gauge images. The reported result is that a deep learning model called ResNet18 reached 97.3% accuracy, while the other two methods reached about 64%.
summary.why: Automatic reading of old analogue instruments could let factories monitor equipment without retrofitting new sensors, which is a practical concern for industrial automation. The text does not say how the accuracy was measured, how the images were split for testing, or how well the results hold for real plant gauges, so the size of the gain should be treated as provisional.

papers.abstract: Analogue gauges remain prevalent in manufacturing industries for measuring physical quantities, yet manual monitoring by operators introduces human error and operational inefficiency. This research developed and evaluated an automated gauge reading system using computer vision and deep learning techniques. Three hybrid approaches were implemented and compared: OpenCV with Scikit-Image (traditional computer vision), OpenCV with ResNet18, and OpenCV with VGG19 (deep learning approaches). A comprehensive dataset of 1,848 pressure gauge images (0-10 BAR range) was curated through web scraping, synthetic generation, and augmentation techniques. The experimental results demonstrate that ResNet18 significantly outperforms the alternatives, achieving an accuracy of 97.3%, compared to VGG19's 64.4% and Scikit-Image's 63.8%. The study validates the effectiveness of residual learning architectures for industrial gauge digitization, providing a robust foundation for Industry 5.0 automation applications.

papers.title: TrajCal: Trajectory-Calibrated Time Schedules for Few-Step Flow Sampling
papers.label: arXiv:2611.25847v1

summary.background:
- Flow matching: a way of training generative models that turns noise into an image or video by following a learned path over time.
- Sampling steps: generation solves this path in many small increments; each increment needs a full neural network pass, so fewer steps means less compute.
- Time schedule: the list of time points at which the steps are taken; changing it changes the result without retraining.
- Few-step sampling: generating with a small number of steps, which is fast but can distort the output.
- Scatter search: a general optimization method that combines and refines a population of candidate solutions.
- Fidelity to a reference: how closely the fast output matches the output of a slow, many-step run.
summary.one_liner: TrajCal is a training-free method that uses scatter search to find one fixed time schedule for few-step flow-matching sampling, chosen to keep outputs closer to a many-step reference for image and video generation.
summary.plain: Modern AI image and video generators build their output by taking many small steps, and each step runs a large neural network, which is slow. This paper looks at how to take fewer steps without the result drifting away from what the slow, full-length process would produce. The authors search for a good fixed set of step timings, reuse it on new inputs, and report higher fidelity to the reference at low step budgets.
summary.why: Faster generation at similar quality matters for making these models cheaper to run. The text reports gains against baselines, but only in the abstract, so the size and consistency of those gains are not yet clear from this summary alone.

papers.abstract: Flow matching enables high-quality image and video generation, but its iterative sampling process requires repeated evaluations of large neural networks. Existing few-step methods can distort the output and reduce its agreement with a many-step reference. We propose TrajCal, a training-free calibration framework for few-step sampling. Based on scatter search, a well-established metaheuristic for difficult optimization problems, TrajCal starts with diverse seed schedules, deforms and combines these candidates, and selects one fixed schedule by final output fidelity for reuse on new inputs. For both image and video generation, TrajCal achieves higher reference fidelity than all compared baselines at low evaluation budgets while maintaining competitive visual quality. The search is effective even with randomly generated seeds, while trajectory-based seeds further improve fidelity. For cross-style generalization, photography-calibrated schedules also improve fidelity on unseen image styles.

papers.title: VideoACE: Benchmarking Agentic Video Understanding through High-Frame-Rate Actions
papers.label: arXiv:2611.24184v1

summary.background:
- Agentic video understanding: a model that can take actions, such as replaying or zooming into a video, instead of only reading it once.
- Frame rate: how many still images per second make up a video; high-frame-rate footage has fast, subtle motion.
- Benchmark: a standard test set used to compare models.
- Temporal evidence annotations: labels marking which moments in the video show the answer.
- User simulator: a scripted stand-in for a human who gives hints or feedback.
- Answer leakage: when a hint accidentally gives away the correct answer; the authors say their hints were screened for this.
summary.one_liner: VideoACE is a benchmark of 1,000 multiple-choice questions on fine-grained high-frame-rate action videos, designed to test whether video models improve when they can actively inspect clips, adjust sampling, and revise answers under simulated user feedback.
summary.plain: Most video AI systems are tested by watching a clip once and answering a question. This paper proposes a test where the model can instead go back, zoom in on particular moments, look at finer detail, and change its answer after hints from a simulated user. The authors tested five models under three setups (one pass, using tools on its own, and using tools with user feedback) to see how each one gathers evidence and whether it makes use of the extra chances to look again.
summary.why: It shifts video evaluation from a fixed one-time view toward measuring how well a model uses interaction, which matters as video AI is increasingly deployed in agent-like roles. The text reports patterns across five models but gives no summary of how large the differences were, so its practical weight is still for specialists to judge.

papers.abstract: Agentic video understanding requires models to actively interact with video environments to gather evidence and form judgments. Evaluating this capability therefore requires assessing whether models can translate opportunities for interaction into better understanding. We introduce VideoACE, a benchmark for assessing video understanding under conditions that support sustained interaction. We focus on high-frame-rate action videos, where rapid, subtle changes make targeted observation especially valuable. The benchmark comprises 1,000 multiple-choice questions spanning six categories of fine-grained action understanding, accompanied by temporal evidence annotations and user hints screened for answer leakage. Its evaluation environment combines video inspection tools with a user simulator, allowing models to adjust temporal coverage, sampling density, and spatial detail, and to revisit evidence and revise their judgments under simulated user feedback. We evaluate single-pass observation, autonomous tool use, and tool use combined with user feedback to examine how effectively models exploit these opportunities. Evaluation of five models reveals distinct patterns in how they acquire evidence and respond to opportunities for further interaction. These findings establish VideoACE as a testbed for examining agentic video understanding beyond performance under a fixed observation setting.

papers.title: SimplePro: A Simple Baseline for Proactive Video Understanding
papers.label: arXiv:2611.23954v1

summary.background:
- Vision-language model (VLM): an AI model that takes images or video frames plus text and produces text.
- Proactive video understanding: the model must choose when to speak during a live video, not only answer when asked.
- Streaming setting: video arrives frame by frame, so the model cannot see the future.
- Training-free / frozen model: the model's weights are not updated; only the prompting and context handling are designed.
- Benchmarks named: OVO-Bench, StreamingBench-PO, ProactiveVideoQA (evaluation suites for this task).
- Backbone size: the number of parameters in the underlying model (2B to 32B here).
- Duplicate filtering: repeated identical answers are suppressed while raw outputs remain as context.
summary.one_liner: SimplePro is a training-free baseline that prompts a frozen 4B vision-language model with explicit reporting rules, recent high-resolution frames, bounded history, and prior answers to decide when to respond in streaming video, reporting gains over specialized proactive systems on three benchmarks.
summary.plain: The paper looks at AI systems that watch a video as it unfolds and must decide on their own when to say something and when to stay quiet. The authors show that a general-purpose vision-language model, used without any retraining, can do this well if it is given clear rules about when to report and a structured memory of what it has already seen and said. They call the resulting method SimplePro and report that it beats more specialized systems on three test suites.
summary.why: Most proactive video systems rely on task-specific training or extra trigger modules, so a strong no-training baseline is useful for judging whether those added parts are needed. Its relevance beyond these benchmarks, such as to live assistants or monitoring tools, is not addressed in the text.

papers.abstract: Proactive video understanding requires vision-language models (VLMs) to decide not only what to answer as a video unfolds, but also when newly arrived evidence warrants a response and when to remain silent. Although modern VLMs excel at offline long-video understanding, they struggle in proactive streaming settings, leading prior work to introduce task-specific reinforcement learning or auxiliary triggering modules. We find that explicit reporting rules and structured streaming context substantially improve a frozen VLM's proactive response performance. We exploit this observation to build SIMPLEPRO, a training-free baseline for proactive video understanding. At each decision step, the model combines recent high-resolution frames, bounded historical observations, and prior answer records to determine whether new information warrants a response and, when needed, generate a concise answer. The system then filters consecutive duplicate answers while retaining the raw outputs as context for subsequent decisions. Without any parameter updates or auxiliary triggers, SIMPLEPRO with a 4B backbone consistently outperforms specialized proactive systems across OVO-Bench, StreamingBench-PO, and ProactiveVideoQA. SIMPLEPRO shows overall performance gains as backbone size increases from 2B to 32B. We hope this simple yet effective method will serve as a strong baseline for proactive video understanding, and we will release our code and inference pipeline to support future research.

papers.title: Tracking Ethological Behaviors of Broiler Chickens Through Computer Vision (YoloV11) Using an Android Mobile Device
papers.label: arXiv:2611.23007v1

summary.background:
- Object detection models (such as YOLO) find and label objects in images or video frames.
- AP (average precision) and precision/recall are standard scores: precision is how often a detection is correct, recall is how many true cases are found.
- Annotation means humans labeling example images so the model can learn from them.
- TFLite is a format that lets trained models run on phones.
- Ethology is the scientific study of animal behavior; broiler chickens are meat-production birds.
- Precision farming uses sensors and data to manage livestock and crops more finely.
summary.one_liner: A YOLOv11 object-detection model was trained on annotated public videos to classify broiler chicken postures (sitting, standing, feeding) and deployed in an Android app via TFLite conversion, with per-class accuracy reported on unseen images.
summary.plain: Farmers need to know how chickens are behaving, since changes in posture or eating can signal welfare problems, but watching thousands of birds by eye is impractical. This paper describes training a computer vision model to recognize three behaviors from videos (sitting, standing, and feeding) and running it on a phone. The model did well on sitting, moderately on standing, and worst on feeding, which is the most movement-based behavior.
summary.why: Automated, low-cost monitoring of animal behavior could support earlier welfare checks on farms, which is the stated motivation. The text is limited, though: it reports per-class scores and small-sample accuracies but gives little detail on dataset size, test conditions, or how well results would hold on commercial farms, so the practical value is still unproven.

papers.abstract: This study developed and evaluated a computer vision model for automated ethological behavior classification of broiler chickens in climate-controlled poultry houses. Using publicly available videos preprocessed and manually annotated into three classes (sitting, standing, and feeding), the YOLOv11 model was trained and deployed on an Android application via TFLite conversion. Exploratory analysis ensured dataset consistency and visual quality, while evaluation showed class-dependent performance: higher robustness for static postures (sitting, AP=0.531; precision=100%) and lower accuracy for dynamic behaviors (feeding, AP=0.292; recall=0.20). Tests with unseen images demonstrated significant improvements, achieving accuracies of 98.04% for sitting, 83.33% for standing, and 67.65% for feeding. The model showed effective generalization in real farm environments, supporting its potential for continuous behavioral monitoring, early welfare assessments, and decision-making in precision poultry farming. These findings establish a technical foundation for future mobile-based applications at commercial scale, reinforcing the role of computer vision in automated animal welfare evaluation.

papers.title: Visual Harness Scales General VLMs to Medical Images
papers.label: arXiv:2611.22815v2

summary.background:
- Vision-language model (VLM): an AI system that takes images and text as input and answers in text.
- Agentic loop: the model repeatedly acts (for example, inspects an image), checks results, and revises its answer.
- Harness: the software scaffolding around a model that supplies tools, memory, and feedback, without changing the model's weights.
- Lossless memory: a store that keeps all gathered findings intact for later use.
- Medical imaging modalities: the types of scans, such as CT or X-ray; the paper covers four.
- Benchmarks are reported as percentage accuracy; the text does not describe the datasets in detail.
summary.one_liner: VERA is a medical "visual harness" that wraps general vision-language models in interactive image tools and an evidence memory, and reports gains across 11 medical imaging tasks.
summary.plain: General AI models that read both pictures and text often struggle with medical scans. This paper proposes a wrapper, called VERA, that lets such a model zoom in, take measurements, and keep notes on what it has found. It then reviews its own answer and goes back to look again until it has enough evidence.
summary.why: The paper reports large gains on some tasks, such as detecting pulmonary nodules (small spots in the lung), for both an open model and a commercial API model. It suggests that the surrounding tooling around a model may matter as much as the model itself, though the text gives no independent validation or clinical testing.

papers.abstract: We show that an appropriate visual harness can substantially improve the performance of general vision-language models (VLMs) across diverse medical imaging tasks. We introduce VERA, a medical visual harness that equips general VLMs with interactive visual tools and systematic diagnostic evidence management. With VERA, general VLMs interactively explore medical images and progressively acquire diagnostic evidence, which is preserved in a lossless memory for subsequent retrieval and use. After submitting an initial answer, the VLM receives an assessment of potential omissions and the reliability of identified findings. This assessment guides further image inspection and measurement, followed by answer revision in an iterative agentic loop until sufficient evidence is obtained. Across 11 tasks and four imaging modalities, VERA improves performance on all tasks with Qwen3.8-27B, with notable gains in spleen measurement (63.3% to 98.3%), renal search (57.5% to 71.2%), and pulmonary nodule detection (0.0% to 28.2%). High-capability API-based VLMs achieve even higher performance with VERA. For example, GPT-6.1 Sol improves pulmonary nodule detection from 10.8% to 69.2% with VERA, demonstrating the complementary benefits of stronger model capabilities and an effective medical visual harness. Our results highlight the potential of visual harnesses as a new paradigm for scaling general VLMs to medical imaging tasks.
